notes:
I found good coverage of the traditional reading for most verses. Protestant traditions don't differ much here; the real debates are about apparent mismatches with the Old Testament (vv. 2–4, 6, 14, 16) and who the "angel" in v. 30 was. I couldn't find any notes for vv. 11–13 and 18–19, any modern-scholarship pages (bibleodyssey or netbible), any Orthodox page, or any prosperity or hyper-grace teaching on this passage, so those are left out.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview.** Stephen's history lesson makes two points: God never limited Himself to one place, such as the temple, and Israel has a habit of rejecting the people God sends. Guzik: Stephen stressed things the Sanhedrin "may not have considered: That God never confined Himself to one place (like the temple), and that the Jewish people had a habit of rejecting those God sends to them." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-7-commentary). Utley lists three answers to the charges: God acted outside the temple, God works with Gentiles, and the Jews have always rejected God's messengers, now including the Messiah. (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)

**v. 1:** Guzik says the high priest was probably still Caiaphas, who had presided at Jesus' trial. He adds that this speech is less a defence than a declaration of the truth about Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/) The Catholic Encyclopedia suggests the accusers twisted things Stephen had really said, such as that God does not live in houses made by hands, and Jesus' prediction that the temple would be destroyed. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14286b.htm)

**v. 2:**
- God's glory appeared to Abraham before he entered the Promised Land. So neither the temple nor the land was needed for God to reveal Himself. Guzik quotes Stott calling Him a "pilgrim God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)
- Barnes thinks the word "glory" was partly meant to answer the charge that Stephen had blasphemed God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-2.htm)
- Ellicott links this opening "God of glory" to the end of the speech, where Stephen sees that glory belonging to the Son of Man. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/7.htm)
- Wiersbe (quoted by Precept Austin) says Abraham was saved by grace through faith, not by circumcision, law-keeping or temple worship. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-7-commentary)

**vv. 2–3, Ur or Haran?** Genesis 12 seems to place God's call in Haran, while Stephen places it in Mesopotamia. Precept Austin's view is that Stephen "telescopes" accounts, and that saying God "appeared" adds detail rather than contradicting Genesis. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-7-commentary) Barnes points out that Genesis 15:7, Joshua 24:3 and Nehemiah 9:7 say God brought Abraham from Ur. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-2.htm)

**vv. 3–4:**
- Guzik reads Abraham's stop in Haran with his father as partial obedience. The promise was on hold, not cancelled, and Abraham *grew* in faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)
- On "after his father died," Utley notes that Genesis 11:26, 32 and 12:4 seem not to add up. He gives two possible answers, citing Archer: Abraham was listed first because he was the most famous son, not the oldest, or the Samaritan Pentateuch's figure for Terah's age at death (145) is correct. (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)

**v. 5:** Abraham had neither land nor child and could only trust God. Guzik says he stayed a pilgrim and didn't make idols of God's blessings, which was a rebuke to leaders who idolised the temple and the land. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/) Utley points to Genesis 15:6 on Abraham's faith. (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)

**vv. 6–7:** Guzik: God knows how to protect His people. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/) Utley explains why Stephen says 400 years when Exodus 12:40 says 430. Rabbis counted from the offering of Isaac, Calvin called 400 a round number, and it may mean four generations. He adds that "in this place" (v. 7) comes from Exodus 3:12. (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)

**v. 8:** Circumcision became the sign of the covenant, handed down through the patriarchs. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/) Precept Austin says circumcision meant something different to the Sanhedrin than it had to the patriarchs. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-7-commentary)

**vv. 9–10:** "God was with him" in Egypt, with no temple. Guzik sees Joseph as a picture of Jesus, a brother rejected by his family who later became their saviour. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

**v. 14:** Genesis 46:27 says 70; Stephen follows the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament), which says 75. Guzik says the Septuagint isn't wrong, just counting differently, by adding five more descendants of Joseph born in Egypt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/) Utley notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls also read 75. (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)

**vv. 15–16:**
- Genesis records two purchases: Abraham bought Machpelah at Hebron, and Jacob bought a field at Shechem. Precept Austin gives possible solutions: Abraham made an earlier purchase at Shechem, Stephen compressed the two stories, or Jacob bought the land in Abraham's name. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-7-commentary)
- Bible Hub's Q&A says property was often credited to the head of a clan. (https://biblehub.com/q/who_bought_shechem's_burial_site,_abraham_or_jacob.htm)
- Utley suggests Abraham may have bought the field at Shechem (Genesis 12:6–7) and Jacob later bought it back. (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)
- Guzik: this burial plot was the only land Abraham ever owned in Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)
- Ellicott thinks Stephen's focus on Shechem, by then a Samaritan town, may have angered his hearers. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-16.htm)

**vv. 17–22:** Guzik sees Moses as like Jesus: favoured by God from birth, protected as a child, pleasing to God without temple or ritual (v. 20), and wise and mighty in words and deeds (v. 22). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

**v. 23:** At the set time Moses left his royal position out of care for his people, another parallel with Jesus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)

**vv. 24–25:**
- Ellicott translates "and he supposed" rather than "for he supposed." He says "for" makes the killing look more deliberate than Exodus 2 does, and he reads the act as a first step toward deliverance. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-25.htm)
- Barnes: Exodus doesn't say what Moses supposed, but it is quite likely. (same page)
- Trapp: long oppression had made the Israelites nearly forget God's promise. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/act-7.cfm)
- Bible Hub's study notes describe a repeated pattern of rejecting God's deliverers, from Joseph to the prophets to Christ. (https://biblehub.com/acts/7-25.htm)

**vv. 26–29:** Israel rejected Moses spitefully. Guzik's application: "you have rejected Jesus, who is like Moses but greater, and denied His right to be ruler and judge." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/) Bible Hub's notes see the 40 years in Midian as a setback that became preparation. (https://biblehub.com/acts/7-25.htm)

**v. 30:**
- Again God appears outside the land, before any temple existed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-7/)
- Gill says the angel was the Son of God, "an uncreated angel." Several older commentators on the Bible Hub page see the unburnt bush as Israel in suffering but not destroyed. Ellicott says this passage also answered the charge that Stephen had spoken against Moses. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-30.htm)

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**How to handle the mismatches (vv. 2–4, 6, 14, 16).**
- Precept Austin quotes MacArthur: charging Luke or Stephen with error "has serious implications for the doctrine of inspiration." So it looks for ways to reconcile the texts. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-7-commentary)
- Utley also affirms the Bible's accuracy, but says Stephen may have been retelling what he learned in synagogue school or adapting texts for his purpose. Fixating on details reflects modern ideas of history-writing. (https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-7)
- Ellicott calls v. 16 an apparent "direct contradiction" and turns to textual criticism. Another commentator on the same page says the error slipped from Stephen's memory in an unprepared speech. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-16.htm)
- I couldn't find denominational sources that frame this as a Baptist vs. Methodist (and so on) dispute.

**Who was the angel (v. 30)?**
- The Reformed Geneva Study Bible says it was the Son of God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-30.htm)
- Calvin compares the burning bush to the way sacraments work: God links a sign to the thing it means. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/7-30.html)
- Constable says it was very possibly the pre-incarnate Christ. The Contending for the Faith commentary disagrees with Lenski and Barnes and rejects that view. (same page)

## 3. Other views

**Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia and catholic.com add background. It hasn't been proven that Stephen studied under Gamaliel, and the charges against him were twisted versions of things he had actually taught. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14286b.htm; https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/stephen-martyr-saint)

**Jewish tradition (cited by Gill on v. 30):** Many Jewish writers took the angel to be "the angel the Redeemer." The Targum of Jonathan seems to treat him as a created angel, and others named Michael or Gabriel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-30.htm)
